text:
The text contrasts two opposing views on human nature: the inherent evil within humans versus the idea that society corrupts an inherently good and free individual.

Similarities in presentation include the use of specific literary and philosophical references to support each viewpoint. Both arguments are grounded in established works—William Golding’s novel Lord of the Flies for the theme of inherent evil, and Jean-Jacques Rousseau’s philosophy for the theme of societal corruption. Additionally, both sides use the concept of a "natural state" as a point of comparison, though they define it differently.

Differences in presentation lie in the source and nature of the evidence. Golding’s perspective is presented through a narrative example, illustrating how boys descend into savagery when removed from societal constraints, thereby suggesting that evil is internal. In contrast, Rousseau’s perspective is presented through a philosophical quote and abstract reasoning, arguing that external forces (society) impose "chains" on an otherwise free and good human nature. Thus, one relies on fictional narrative to demonstrate internal decay, while the other relies on philosophical assertion to highlight external corruption.
